news.title: Three in five Americans favor stronger oversight of social media companies, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
news.text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 9 (Reuters) - A bipartisan ⁠majority of Americans support more government rules for how social media companies conduct business, including a requirement of age-verification tools to keep younger children off social ⁠media, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. 

The poll, which was conducted over the six days ending August 3, comes as companies like Meta Platforms and ‌Google's YouTube face mounting legal pressure over their treatment of young users. A trial is expected to begin on Wednesday over allegations by state prosecutors that Meta designed its products to addict young users. 

Meta, which denies the allegations, says it could face up to $1.4 trillion in penalties if the states prevail. A New Mexico state court on Thursday separately ordered Meta to pay $567 million into a teen mental health fund and change ​how its platforms function for young users, after finding the company is to blame for harming children's wellbeing. 

Tech ⁠companies are also under increasing scrutiny by lawmakers across the U.S. ⁠for their effect on youth. More than a dozen states have passed laws regulating minors' social media access, saying it is needed to bolster their safety online. NetChoice, ⁠a ‌trade group backed by social media giants such as Meta, TikTok and Snap, has sued to stop laws requiring apps verify the ages of their users. It argues such laws violate free speech protections. 

Some 61% of poll respondents - including 71% of Democrats and 62% of Republicans - said social media companies need firmer oversight. Support among independents ⁠was lower as many of them said they were unsure where they stood.

The poll also found ​66% support laws that would require social media companies ‌use age-verification tools to keep children under age 16 from accessing their platforms. Support was highest among Republicans, with 74% backing the idea, compared to 69% ⁠of Democrats.

'SOMEBODY'S GOT TO DO ​IT'

James Bosserdet, a 60-year-old mechanical engineer from Tennessee who voted for Republican President Donald Trump in the 2024 election, said he mostly wants the U.S. government to have a smaller role in Americans' lives, but that cracking down on social media companies is an exception. 

"Somebody's got to do it," he said, referring to setting restrictions on social media for kids. "Is it the government's job? I don't want ⁠it to be. I think maybe it should be."

The U.S. Congress has so far not passed ​legislation aimed at protecting kids on social media. 

An overwhelming majority of Americans - 85% - think social media can be addictive for children, and a similar share think its use can be harmful for their mental health, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Washington, D.C., resident Christopher Chen, 34, said he thinks social media companies have an outsized influence on teens, adding that the tech ⁠firms have too much control over what their users see on their apps. 

"I don't know what the regulation looks like, but something needs to be done by the government to protect the people," said Chen, who voted for Trump's 2024 Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

Paula Dick, 73, said social media companies could do a better job keeping kids away from inappropriate content, adding that there should be more government oversight of the apps they use. Dick said she doesn't allow her grandchildren to use YouTube when she watches them, but they ​have found ways to access it anyway. Dick, who lives in Kansas, voted for Trump in 2024.

"They have workarounds to get ⁠around blocks that their parents have put on their phones," she said. "They're pretty intelligent when it comes to that."

USERS LIKE SOCIAL MEDIA

But Americans also say they like social media a ​lot, with 70% saying their time spent on the platforms is fun, while only 35% say it stressed them ‌out. People are split on whether they are overdoing it, with 52% saying they ​spend too much time every day on social media, and 43% saying that's not the case. 

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, surveyed 4,505 U.S. adults and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points in either direction. 

 (Reporting by Jason Lange and Courtney Rozen; editing by Scott Malone and Deepa Babington)
news.author: Courtney Rozen,Jason Lange

news.title: Primary night was full of close races, surprise winners — and Madonna
news.text:
Michigan's 2026 seemingly interminable primary season is — finally — over.

We had to wait an extra day to find out who won the closely-contested Democratic U.S. Senate primary, but before you get too comfy, it's time to face the reality that elections are like pesky reporters: Every answer begets more questions.

Abdul El-Sayed answered the question of whether the Democratic wave of progressive candidates would wash away another establishment candidate, but his victory in the Michigan U.S. Senate primary raises questions about whether either of Detroit's two most recent mayors are going to get involved in the campaign, the accuracy of polling and the value of endorsements, and whether a very different "uncommitted" movement than the one that kneecapped Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 could hinder El-Sayed's ambitions.

John James answered the question of how much value President Donald Trump's endorsement has in a Michigan Republican primary, but the number of voters who cast ballots for candidates who dropped out of the race and endorsed James raises questions about his popularity among Michigan GOP voters.

This is weighty stuff, people!

If you believe the pundits who use terms like "inflection point" and "existential crisis" so often that the phrases now sound funny, the fate of the Great State of Michigan and the very Republic itself hinge on the answers to these questions.

Before I let you get back to more pressing questions — like whether the Tigers still have a chance to make the playoffs after trading away their two best pitchers — we'll also touch on less portentous topics including:

"How did a congressional candidate who dropped out of his primary — and endorsed a rival — end up winning his race by double digits?" and "Which Madonna song — which you might consider the least likely to hear at a victory party for a candidate who wants to get the big money out of politics — got a spin while supporters waited for election results?"

For answers to those questions and more, Gentle Reader, read on ... !

Conspicuously absent

El-Sayed's victory over U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, of Birmingham, was especially impressive when you consider that Stevens beat El-Sayed in Michigan's most populous counties of Wayne, Oakland and Macomb.

Drilling down even deeper, Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, of Royal Oak, got nearly twice as many votes in Detroit as El-Sayed. Stevens and McMorrow, who dropped out before Election Day but not in time to get her name off the ballot, received 64,897 votes in Detroit — or nearly 66 percent of the vote — compared with El-Sayed's 33,786 votes, which amounted to just over 34 percent of ballots cast.

While big-name Democrats across Michigan signed on to Stevens' campaign, Detroit's most successful and prominent progressive politician — Mayor Mary Sheffield — stayed out of the race.

That didn't stop El-Sayed from trying to bask in a bit of the mayor's reflected glory by dropping her name in his news release announcing that her father, the Rev. Horace Sheffield III, had endorsed him. The third paragraph of the campaign's Nov. 13, 2025 bulletin highlighted that Sheffield is the "proud father of Detroit Mayor-elect Mary Sheffield."

The news release also noted that the Rev. Sheffield "holds key leadership roles" with multiple organizations, including the Detroit Ecumenical Ministers Alliance.

Perhaps coincidentally, El-Sayed's campaign made the first of at least seven $7,500 payments to the alliance on Oct. 21 — three weeks before the Rev. Sheffield publicly announced his support of El-Sayed. According to the most recent campaign finance reports available, El-Sayed's campaign has paid the alliance $52,500 for consulting.

Assuming those monthly payments continued after the March 2 disbursement listed in the period covered by the campaign finance report, the alliance collected another $37,500 before Tuesday's Aug. 4 primary election. If those monthly payments continue through the Nov. 3 general election, the alliance could receive up to $112,500 by the time the race is done.

With the exception of the 2025 mayor's race — when the Rev. Sheffield campaigned with his daughter, was involved in advertising purchases and played a leadership role on the mayor's transition team — the mayor has emphasized throughout her political career that she is independent from her father.

With or without the Rev. Sheffield's help, El-Sayed surely will be working to win over the mayor to improve on his paltry performance in Michigan's richest trove of Democratic votes.

Hizzoner on hiatus

Days after Mike Duggan dropped his independent bid for governor in May, I asked him whether he expected to support other candidates. He said he would decide in the fall whether to get involved in any races.

Duggan will have plenty of familiar faces to choose from.

He hired El-Sayed to run the city's health department, worked with Attorney General nominee Eli Savit and Secretary of State nominee Garlin Gilchrist II in Detroit city hall, and made gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson's husband Ryan Friedrichs his chief development officer during his first term as mayor. (After five years, Friedrichs left in 2020 for a job in the private sector.)

Based on the number of people who have told me their biggest complaint about the primary election was that Duggan's name would not be on the ballot, the former three-term Detroit mayor could play a pivotal role in winning over voters — especially the coveted independents who often decide elections.

But I'm told Duggan is, as the kids say, "living his best life."

More: I watched every Michigan debate so you don't have to. Here's what I learned.

Hizzoner is traveling and spending time with family and appears to be in no hurry to return to the political fray, where he excelled for more than 40 years.

He told me back in May that he would evaluate candidates and might help state House and Senate hopefuls who espouse his anti-partisan, problem-solving message. I asked him if there was any chance he would not endorse a Democrat, figuring that even though he left the Democratic Party to run for governor as an independent he would still lean more blue than red.

"I'm going to wait and see how the candidates are in the fall," he said. "And who wants my support and who's running the campaigns about what they're going to accomplish."

Few politicians hold their cards closer to the vest than Duggan, but it's possible he may keep his peace throughout a general election campaign that will likely be prodigiously polluted with the kind of partisan politics he now pooh-poohs.

The eternal question

Political junkies love horse race polls and politicians covet endorsements from elected officials.

I've never put much stock in either.

I didn't do any polling when I ran for Detroit City Council back in 2021, but people connected to pollsters occasionally shared intel that I was either last or first in the latest sounding. I suspect these whispers were meant to entice me to hire the pollsters, but in the end the candidate who finished first in the polls where I ranked last didn't even make it through the primary. I finished second in that election, which is the only poll that really matters. Detroit municipal elections are nonpartisan, so I advanced to the general election ... where voters overwhelmingly endorsed my return to journalism.

Highly-touted polls conducted in the homestretch of the Democratic U.S. Senate primary showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Stevens. In the end, the good doctor won by less than one percentage point.

By then, Stevens had won the support of two former Michigan governors, our current governor, a beloved former U.S. Senator, and the popular senator she was running to replace.

So were the pollsters wrong — or did the results motivate independents and undecided voters to rally for Stevens?

Were the endorsements useless — or did the last-minute blessings of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Sen. Gary Peters help virtually eliminate El-Sayed's massive lead?

Beats me, but this much I know: Democracy works best when you do your homework and make up your own mind.

Uncommitted — with a twist?

Democratic skepticism and, in many cases, outright hostility toward President Joe Biden's handling of the war in Gaza cost Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris tens of thousands of votes she needed to win Michigan in 2024.

Democrats who abandoned the party declared themselves "uncommitted" and declined to cast a ballot for Harris. Others voted for third party candidates or Republican Donald Trump. Many of those voters live in cities like Dearborn, which have large populations who hail from the Middle East.

For months, we've heard that some of those same voters might not support Stevens if she won the Democratic U.S. Senate nomination, because of her support for Israel and the tens of millions spent on her behalf by a political action committee associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Some Democrats speculated that Stevens could suffer the same fate as Harris.

Those fears were allayed when El-Sayed won a staggering 78% of the vote in Dearborn.

Now, some Democrats are concerned Jewish voters and others offended by El-Sayed's call for an end to U.S. military spending on Israel will mount their own uncommitted effort in the U.S. Senate race or, worse, vote for Republican Mike Rogers.

To gauge the potential peril for El-Sayed, I turned to Mark Grebner of Practical Political Data, who I'm sure has spent more time studying Michigan voting data than anyone in our state's 189-year history.

Grebner is a Democrat, but his expertise is acknowledged by pols on every point of the political compass.

He offered several observations that should give El-Sayed some peace.

First, he says Arab American voters outnumber Jewish voters in Michigan. While Grebner said Arab American voters tend to favor Republicans, political attacks on El-Sayed, a Muslim whose family emigrated from Egypt, combined with the wars in Gaza and Iran has turned them, at least temporarily, into reliable Democratic voters.

Second, he says Jewish voters tend to favor Democrats, and a significant portion of those voters are also critical of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Grebner also says that his analysis of results in certain down ballot races persuades him that 47.5% of Michigan voters favor Democrats and 42.5% favor Republicans, with the remaining 10% splitting their ticket.

If he's right, Republicans need to win over three out of every four ticket-splitters to overcome the Democrats' built-in 5% advantage.

That's some mighty high-falutin' thinking for my little brain, but primary voting totals suggest El-Sayed could lose some hardcore Stevens and Israel supporters and still have an advantage over Rogers.

Rogers got virtually all of the 880,000 votes in the Republican U.S. Senate primary.

El-Sayed got only 741,000 votes in the Democratic U.S. Senate primary, but nearly 1.5 million Democrats voted in that race. So he should be in good shape as long as he wins over a nice chunk of the 787,000 people who voted for Stevens and McMorrow.

Some pundits believe you can't compare red and blue turnout because the Democratic U.S. Senate primary was so fiercely contested, but the Republican gubernatorial primary was way feistier than the Democratic governor's race — and there were still only 929,000 votes cast in the GOP primary while Dems, again, collected 1.5 million votes.

The caveat is that primaries have much lower turnout than general elections.

Still, Democrats have got to feel good that their candidates got 50% more votes than Republicans in the top races.

Lame James?

A win is a win, but Republican gubernatorial nominee John James can't be thrilled that his opponents — including two who dropped out of the race and endorsed him — got more primary votes than he did.

James, a congressman from Shelby Township, got 465,000 votes.

Businessman Perry Johnson, former Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox, state Senate Republican Leader Aric Nesbitt and write-in candidates combined to collect a hair more than 50% of all votes cast in the GOP primary.

Cox, who dropped out less than three weeks before the polls closed, got a surprising 13% of the vote. Nesbitt, who dropped out six weeks ago after Trump endorsed James, got about 2% of the vote.

This could be a sign James will need to work hard to win over large chunks of the Republican base at the same time he woos independent voters to build a winning coalition.

He should enjoy one advantage over his Democratic opponent, however.

While Benson faced little opposition from Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, James is battle-tested after a vigorously-contested race in which he performed well in debates where Cox and Johnson tried to destroy him.

Don't try this at home

If you count my time at the college newspaper, I've been covering politics and government for nearly 40 years — but I've never seen a candidate pull off the kind of victory Thomas Smith, of Flint, celebrated on Tuesday.

Smith won the Republican nomination to challenge U.S. Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, of Bay City, less than a month after dropping out of the race and endorsing another candidate. Smith, unintentionally, also overcame Trump's endorsement one of his former rivals, Amir Hassan.

Smith's campaign had put up a nice website, but he claimed in a handwritten letter he sent to the Federal Election Commission that he couldn't file a proper campaign finance report because he couldn't log into their system and had "not been able to get a response from the help desk." In any case, he said he only raised $1,850.

Nevertheless, Smith won the three-way primary with more than 50% of the vote.

Al Lemmo, the candidate Smith eventually endorsed when he dropped out of the race in mid-July, finished last with 16% of the vote.

Lemmo told the New York Times his campaign's attacks on Hassan, who had won Trump's support and finished second with 33% of the vote, may have backfired.

He said his staff created ads that “didn’t so much appeal to bigotry against Muslims as kind of counted on it,” adding, “But I really didn’t like that because I live in a community with a lot of Muslims. They’re really nice.”

Various media reports said Hassan was a Muslim who converted to Christianity. The Times reported that Hassan said he “studied other faiths” but was a Christian.

Lemmo had also questioned the sincerity of Hassan's recent conversion to the GOP, calling him a "lifelong Democrat" and a "Trojan horse."

Without a hint of irony, Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters congratulated Smith for becoming the GOP's nominee in the 8th Congressional District after "a hard-fought, well-earned primary victory."

Because Smith dropped out too late to get his name off the primary ballot, he will represent the GOP in the general election. And, this time, he's indicated there's no turning back.

Smith updated his website last week with a statement that said he is "humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet" and that he looks forward to working with GOP leaders "to expand our House majority and advance President Trump's America First agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again."

Here's hoping he hears back from the help desk before his next campaign finance report is due.

Name that tune

The wait for results in the Democratic U.S. Senate primary may have run so late that the deejay ran out of options — or maybe the El-Sayed campaign just has a healthy sense of humor — but I couldn't help chuckling as supporters of the campaign that wants to get “money out of politics,” were treated to Madonna's “Material Girl” over the sound system around midnight as we waited for El-Sayed to finally take the stage at the Majestic Theatre.

Several hours later, after everyone had gone home, we learned that their love, and votes, had pushed El-Sayed over the "Borderline" — and on to the general election contest with Rogers.

M.L. Elrick is a Pulitzer Prize- and Emmy Award-winning investigative reporter, director of student investigative reporting program Eye On Michigan, and host of the ML's Soul of Detroit podcast. Contact him at mlelrick@freepress.com or follow him on X at @elrick, Facebook at ML Elrick and Instagram at ml_elrick

news.title: California may fine content creators who don't disclose they were paid to post about politics
news.text: Weeks before voting ended in California's primary for governor, Los Angeles-based influencer Shaka Smith took to Instagram to tell his more than 700,000 followers whom he was voting for and why. “Healthcare shouldn't bankrupt you, housing should not feel impossible, polluters shouldn't pass their bill to us, and artists should not be replaced by AI," Smith said. "That’s why I’m supporting Tom Steyer for governor.” But Smith started the video with a disclaimer: “This is an ad, and honestly, I wish more political content said that first." His caption specified that he was paid by Steyer's campaign. California is one of two states, along with Texas, that have passed policies requiring content creators to say if they've been paid by a political campaign to post, and the Golden State is considering cracking down by fining people who don't. Campaigns have long worked with celebrities and major influencers to win over voters, but now they are teaming up with smaller creators — sometimes with fewer than 100,000 followers — to reach more tailored audiences. That has sparked debates about whether disclosure rules for political advertisements should apply to content creators, who are expected to play prominent roles in the upcoming midterms and the 2028 presidential election. “If you’re running for president and you are not currently trying to court some of these people or lining up your own people to act as surrogates for you, you’re already behind,” said Mike Nellis, a Democratic strategist who worked for Kamala Harris' presidential campaign. Questions about transparency have been fueled by high-profile instances of influencers making content intended to change minds or votes without disclosing they were being paid. In 2022, the campaign of Democratic then-Senate candidate John Fetterman paid Nicole “Snooki” Polizzi of “Jersey Shore” to record a video teasing his GOP rival for leaving New Jersey before announcing his run in Pennsylvania. In 2023, content creators were paid by an influencer marketing agency with conservative ties to defend Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton, a Republican, after he was impeached for alleged bribery and other accusations of misconduct, according to the Texas Tribune. The payments weren’t clearly disclosed in either case. Steyer, a Democratic billionaire who spent more than $215 million of his own money on his unsuccessful bid for governor, took fire from rivals for paying content creators. He wasn’t the only contender in the race paying influencers, but he faced much of the blowback because he had already been accused of trying to buy the election for having poured much of his personal fortune into his campaign. Many of the creators who worked with Steyer’s campaign disclosed that they were paid, but the state’s campaign finance watchdog is investigating several other instances in which creators allegedly didn't. Sen. Adam Schiff of California introduced federal legislation last month, but it hasn't received a vote yet. Some outside groups are urging the Federal Election Commission to pass its own rule. California's law requiring disclosure, passed in 2023, is difficult to enforce. The state’s campaign watchdog can seek a court order compelling an influencer to disclose that they were paid, but that can take months. That prompted Assemblymember Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park) to write a new bill to penalize content creators and political committees if the creator fails to state they were compensated. The bill would give the state’s Fair Political Practices Commission the power to fine influencers and committees if they are found to have violated the law, allowing the commission to bypass the court process. They could face fines of up to $5,000 per violation, according to the commission. “Voters should have a right to know whether or not campaigns are paying for the messaging that they’re seeing,” Berman said. Texas’ campaign watchdog passed a rule in 2024 requiring content creators to include disclaimers when they are paid for political advertisements, and the New York Legislature is considering a similar requirement. Other disclosure bills failed in recent years in Utah and Georgia. Smith, the L.A. influencer, hadn’t committed to a candidate for governor when a trusted friend told him to look into Steyer. That friend had been paid to post about Steyer. Smith liked Steyer’s promise to increase taxes on billionaires and his refusal to accept donations from corporate political action committees. He ended up doing two paid ads, both of which included compensation disclaimers that the Steyer campaign told him were a requirement. Smith wouldn't say exactly how much the campaign paid him, but he said it was in the thousands of dollars. He thinks the posts had an effect on his followers, with only a few detractors objecting. “They kind of trust my voice,” he said of his audience. “They knew that if I’m saying it, it’s at least something they should look into.” Dustin Torreverde, a content creator in Southern California who hasn’t been paid by a political campaign for social media posts, said it's important for influencers to be transparent with their audiences. But the bill could pose an unfair burden on creators who are just trying to make a living, he said. “A lot of us are very small creators,” he said. “So if we were to get penalized and we have to get lawyers, stuff like that, it’s going to be very difficult for us.” Adina Flores, a libertarian content creator in Northern California who votes for both parties, said influencers should have to disclose if they are paid and that she generally supports penalties. She worries some people may take money to post political content without doing a “deep dive into the candidate to make sure that’s somebody they should support.” Saurav Ghosh, a lawyer with the Campaign Legal Center, a nonprofit focused on protecting American democracy, hopes disclosure requirements passed by states will lead to federal rules. “Transparency is one of the most important pillars of our election system,” he said. Austin writes for the Associated Press.
news.summary: California and other states are debating whether to crack down on social media influencers making political advertisements without disclosing that they were paid.
news.author: Sophie Austin

news.text: Some Taylor Swift songs have been removed from social media videos posted by US President Donald Trump's campaign and the White House, which have used two of the American superstar's songs over the past week.The White House and a representative for Swift did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Swift has not spoken recently about Trump, although she endorsed his Democratic rival, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, in 2024.During the 2020 campaign, Swift posted on social media that Trump was "WELL AWARE we do not want him as our president."Trump has repeatedly criticized Swift. It referenced famous songs by the pop star.In June, Trump's campaign posted a video on the short-video platform with Swift's new "Toy Story 5" song "I Knew It, I Knew You." The short video was captioned "Nobody loves our country & the American People more than @President Donald J Trump." It showed him interacting with children at the White House, dancing at a UFC match and appearing at a rally.It was the third time the Trump administration or his campaign had used one of the Grammy Award-winning pop star's songs in recent months.In April, the White House shared a video showing the Artemis II crew meeting with Trump at the White House the day before. The video used Swift's "High Infidelity" and lyrics from the song: "Do you really want to know where I was April 29th?"The White House shared another TikTok video in November featuring "The Fate of Ophelia" from Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl" album, which had been released the month before. That video featured images of the US flag, monuments and various photos of Trump, including his 2023 arrest mugshot.That post garnered widespread social media reaction and led to a White House spokesperson telling multiple news outlets the video was created because the Trump administration knew news outlets "would breathlessly amplify them."The communications team for Trump, who is prolific on social media, has posted an array of hit songs with images including Trump's immigration crackdown, US military operations against Iran and the arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

news.title: What Happened to Trump the Islamophobe?
news.text: President Donald Trump has spent his second term doing things that once would have revived a defining refrain from his first presidency—he is hostile to Muslims. But, “Trump the Islamophobe” no longer carries the same political force it once did. One of the likely reasons that refrain has quieted is that Trump is harder to place inside that old frame: He still uses inflammatory rhetoric and pursues restrictive immigration policies, but he has also built closer ties with some Muslim-majority governments while going to war with another, and he won support from a larger share of Muslim voters than he did during his first term. That makes the politics less straightforward than they were in 2017. Back then, Trump entered office after calling in 2015 for a “total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States.” He went on to restrict entry from several Muslim-majority countries, while insisting the policy was about terrorism and not religion. The Supreme Court ultimately upheld a later version of the restrictions in 2018. The political identity stuck. In a 2017 Pew Research Center survey, 74 percent of Muslim Americans described Trump as “unfriendly” toward them, while only 19 percent approved of his presidency. Just 8 percent of Muslim voters told Pew they had cast a ballot for him. The Democratic Party organized itself around the charge. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wept on camera denouncing the travel ban and moved within days to repeal it by legislation. Nine years later, Trump has supplied plenty of material for critics to make the same accusation. The difference is that the political coalition around him no longer makes the charge quite as simple. Trump Hasn’t Stopped Giving Critics Ammunition Trump has hardly stopped giving his critics material on this issue. After the November 2025 shooting of National Guard members, allegedly by an Afghan national, in Washington, D.C., the administration tightened immigration restrictions, later expanding entry limits covering dozens of countries, many of them Muslim-majority. The proclamation that took effect January 1 fully restricted entry from 19 countries and partially restricts 20 more, along with holders of Palestinian Authority travel documents. The State Department froze immigrant visa processing for nationals of 75 countries three weeks later. The president also returned to explicitly inflammatory rhetoric, calling Somalia “barely a country” and describing Muslim Representative Ilhan Omar and others as “garbage.” In July he shared a post mocking hijab-wearing kindergartners at a St. Paul charter school, which afterward reported threats. Then he went to war. On February 28, American and Israeli forces launched roughly 900 strikes on Iran in 12 hours, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and dozens of other officials. At least 157 people died when a missile hit a girls’ school near a naval base at Minab, according to an estimate by the Associated Press. Trump announced Khamenei’s death on Truth Social, calling him one of the most evil people in history. It was the largest American use of force against a Muslim-majority country in a generation, and almost nobody argued about it in those terms. The Democratic case was constitutional. Senator Tim Kaine forced repeated votes to constrain the president, calling the strikes dangerous and unnecessary. In June, Schumer, Senator Adam Schiff, Kaine and 35 colleagues wrote to Trump disputing his claim that hostilities had ended, calling the war unconstitutional and demanding the Justice Department opinion behind it. Months of bombing produced an argument about the separation of powers. Muslim advocacy groups have continued to describe parts of Trump’s rhetoric and policy as anti-Muslim. The Council on American-Islamic Relations logged 8,683 discrimination complaints in 2025, the most in the 30 years it has published the count, and named Senator Tommy Tuberville an anti-Muslim extremist, the first time it has applied the label to a sitting senator. Dozens of Republican members of Congress belong to a Sharia-Free America caucus. A study published in April counted 1,111 anti-Muslim social media posts by Republican officeholders and eight related bills in 13 months. Public sentiment moved with them. The Islamophobia Index compiled by the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding, which measures endorsement of five false stereotypes about Muslims, rose from 25 in 2022 to 33 in 2025 among the general public, with the steepest increases among white evangelicals and Catholics. One federal measure runs the other way: FBI-reported anti-Muslim hate crime incidents peaked at 307 in 2016 and stood at 228 in 2024. The striking change is not that the accusation has disappeared; it is that it no longer seems to define Trump politically as it did during his first term. Democrats Changed the Words They Use The clearest evidence is legislative, though the trend is not entirely one-way. California Democratic Representative Judy Chu has introduced the NO BAN Act, which would prohibit religious discrimination in immigration decisions, in four consecutive Congresses. The House versions attracted 219 cosponsors in 2019, 159 in 2021, 86 in 2024 and 121 in the current Congress. The House approved the bill’s provisions 233-183 in 2020, with every voting Democrat and two Republicans in favor. By then, Trump’s entry restrictions affected 13 countries. The current proclamation fully restricts entry from 19 countries and partially restricts 20 more, along with holders of Palestinian Authority travel documents. When 61 House Democrats wrote to Trump in February condemning the expansion, they called it “a cruel and racist policy agenda disguised as national security.” The letter did not use the word “Islamophobic.” Individual Democrats made the same substitution. Senator Mark Kelly, asked on Meet the Press about the permanent pause on migration from developing countries, said the administration’s message was that “they don’t want brown people coming to the United States.” Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said Trump had chosen to target “an entire community.” Senator Andy Kim called the June 2025 ban “rooted in bigotry, not security,” then pivoted to prices and health care. Republicans were more specific, which suggests they recognized one of the underlying themes, even if Democrats did not name it. Tuberville called on the government to “IMMEDIATELY BAN all ISLAM immigrants.” Representative Chip Roy posted that the answer was to stop importing Islamists. The contrast with 2017 is hard to miss. Then, Schumer said tears were running down the cheeks of the Statue of Liberty, and Trump mocked him by name the next morning for crying about it. Muslim Voters No Longer Fit the Old Political Story The first complication to the narrative is electoral. Muslim voters remain more Democratic than Republican, but they are no longer easily described as an anti-Trump bloc. The Institute for Social Policy and Understanding found that 50 percent of Muslim voters backed Kamala Harris in 2024, while 31 percent voted for Trump and 12 percent for Jill Stein. Among Muslim men, 42 percent voted for Trump. Other surveys put the split differently. CAIR’s exit poll of 1,575 Muslim voters found Stein at 53 percent, Trump at 21 and Harris at 20. The Associated Press’s VoteCast had Harris at 63 percent. The three agree that Muslim support for Democrats collapsed and disagree about where it went. All of them put Trump well above the 8 percent Pew recorded in 2016. Gaza played an important part in changing the old alignment. Anger over the Biden administration’s support for Israel played a role during the Democratic primary in Michigan, where more than 100,000 voters chose “uncommitted.” Trump later led the field in Dearborn, where Arab and Muslim voters had been an important part of the Democratic coalition. Harris took 36 percent of the vote there, down from nearly 69 percent for Joe Biden four years earlier. (And just two years later, Michigan Democrats voted to send a Muslim candidate into one of America’s biggest Senate races.) That does not mean Muslim voters embraced Trump, because most didn’t, but it does make Islamophobia a more awkward partisan attack when a substantial minority of the voters supposedly targeted by it are willing to vote for him. Trump’s Muslim World Relationships Complicate the Picture Trump’s foreign policy also sits uneasily with the image of a president primarily defined as hostile to Muslims. The first major foreign trip of his second term took him to Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The administration announced a $600 billion Saudi investment commitment, $1.2 trillion in projected economic exchange with Qatar and more than $200 billion in new U.S.-UAE commercial deals. Nine months later he was bombing Tehran. A president who deepens commercial ties with three Muslim-majority monarchies while decapitating the government of a fourth is difficult to assess according to a single religious motive. Close relations with Muslim governments do not answer accusations about Trump’s treatment of Muslims at home. After all, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE are states, not stand-ins for American Muslims. Politically, however, the relationships complicate the picture. Trump can denounce Somali immigrants one month while embracing Arab rulers and courting Muslim voters the next. …Or, Maybe, Americans Are Just Used to Trump There is a simpler explanation for the dialed-back criticism. Exhaustion. Trump has been at the center of American politics for more than a decade. Language that once shocked voters can lose its ability to generate a new political identity when the politician using it is already one of the most familiar people in the country. Search behavior offers partial support. Google Trends data for the United States shows American interest in the phrase “Muslim ban” peaking in January 2017, the month of the first executive order, when it outran searches for “travel ban.” It has not registered a single month anywhere near that level since March 2025. Interest in “travel ban” stayed strong across the same period, rising when Trump restricted 12 countries in June 2025, again in December when he more than doubled the list, and again in February. Americans are still following the policy closely, but appear to have stopped attaching a religion to it. However, there is no clear polling evidence showing that Americans have specifically become tired of accusations of Islamophobia, and the ISPU index points the other way: the sentiment is rising while the political language recedes. Muslim organizations also continue to use the term. In July, for example, CAIR accused Trump of amplifying anti-Muslim bigotry after he shared a social-media post involving Muslim schoolchildren. Democrats use the word too, but about Republicans in Congress and about each other. In March, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Islamophobia “a cancer” after a run of anti-Muslim posts by Republican members. Speaking outside a Bronx mosque last October, days before he was elected mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani said that in an era of vanishing bipartisanship, “Islamophobia has emerged as one of the areas of agreement.” He was describing attacks including by Andrew Cuomo and Eric Adams, both Democrats. The Reverend Al Sharpton, campaigning with him a week later, denounced the “ugly Islamophobia” in the race without naming who was responsible for it. Fatigue is therefore plausible, but difficult to prove. The stronger evidence is that the politics around the accusation have become less simple. What Would Make the Charge Stick Again? The next elections will provide a test. If Muslim voters who moved toward Trump in 2024 turn sharply against Republicans, particularly in Michigan, it would strengthen the argument that his second-term policies have revived the political consequences associated with his first-term rhetoric. Abdul El-Sayed won the state’s Democratic Senate primary this month by about a point against roughly $65 million in outside spending, and the attacks trialed against Mamdani are already being turned on him. The wider ground has shifted too: support for reducing immigration overall has fallen since the 2024 campaign. If Muslim voters remain divided, the lesson may be different: Islamophobia could remain a serious accusation against particular Trump policies or statements without functioning as an all-purpose explanation of his relationship with Muslim Americans. Perhaps that is what happened to “Trump the Islamophobe.” Trump did not change enough to kill the accusation, but the politics changed enough to blunt it: Muslim voters backed him, Muslim governments embraced him and Muslim politicians kept winning. The charge survived. The political reality it once explained did not.
news.summary: Trump still gives critics ammunition on Islam. What changed is the politics: Muslim voters, leaders and governments no longer fit the old frame.
news.author: Anna Rahmanan

news.title: Socialist Francesca Hong on How She'll Win in a State Trump Carried Twice
news.text: Democratic socialist Francesca Hong still picks up bartending shifts. She says that is where she hears the version of the economy that does not show up on cable news. "It's not as simple as putting food on the table," Hong told Newsweek in an exclusive interview. "It's about putting a bill on hold, or you're hearing about more people putting grocery costs on credit, people wondering if they're going to get to go on vacation, people wondering if they're going to get laid off because of AI." Hong, a 37-year-old state representative from Madison and a former restaurant owner, is two days from a Democratic primary for governor that public polling suggests she will win comfortably. She is also running to lead a state President Donald Trump carried in 2016 and again in 2024. Hong and the Pitch Hong entered the race last September as a little-known member of the state Assembly's Socialist Caucus. She now leads every public poll of the primary field. Her platform is built around what she calls "permanent affordability," a phrase that has become a rallying cry for insurgent Democrats since the surprise victory of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in 2025. She says it includes free childcare, fully funding public schools, higher taxes on the ultrawealthy and corporations, and a moratorium on new data centers. "I think you have to launch your campaign thinking that there's always a chance you can win," Hong said. "Here in Wisconsin, I always say that I remain cautiously and sometimes nauseously optimistic that Democrats will continue to win power." She said the stress she hears about while behind the bar does not reduce to talking points. Her answer to that, she said, is organizing. She cited more than 300 events across the state and nearly 50,000 miles traveled. "Our campaign is building a working-class movement demanding better from government," Hong said. She also framed her campaign as a challenge to the Trump administration, saying that if elected she would use "the full force of the executive to protect all Wisconsinites." That stance includes a hard line on immigration enforcement, as Mamdani has done in New York City. "I do not plan on cooperating and working with ICE," she said. Winning in a Purple State Wisconsin has decided its last three presidential elections by roughly a point. Hong argues the state that voted for Trump 21 months ago is not the state she is running in now. "What has changed is that lives have just gotten harder and harder for everyday people across the state," she said, pointing to gas prices, property taxes and grocery bills. She cited the April 7 election in which Chris Taylor won an open seat on the Wisconsin Supreme Court by about 20 percentage points, 60 percent to 40 percent, expanding the court's liberal majority to 5-2. "A double-digit win is a landslide," Hong said. Taylor won a majority in 42 of Wisconsin's 72 counties and flipped suburban Ozaukee County, which then-Vice President Kamala Harris lost with 43.9 percent in 2024. Republicans have argued the comparison does not hold. Turnout in April was about one in three voting-age residents, well below the 2025 court race. However, Hong says the pattern is about anger, not the calendar. "Working class folks are harnessing this frustration and this anger and demanding that there are elected officials in a government that is taking action," she said. "It's about delivering the solutions that actually match the scale and speed in which the struggles of people's lives are growing." The Electability Question Hong's critics have spent the final weeks of the Democratic primary less focused on whether she can win Tuesday than on whether she can win in November. Republicans, rival Democrats and, in the closing stretch, Wisconsin Governor Tony Evers, a Democrat, have questioned whether her progressive record would leave her vulnerable against Wisconsin Representative Tom Tiffany, a Republican. Evers, who said for months he would stay neutral, endorsed Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley three weeks before the primary, after Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez left the race and Crowley reentered it. "I think she's in a tough place. She has spent her entire campaign dealing not with the issues, but what's on the Twitter," Evers told FOX6 Milwaukee on Thursday. Hong said she does not know what Evers tells voters about her but pointed to his earlier comments that she is talented. Her campaign said attention to years-old social media posts had crowded out her policy agenda. Asked about a 2020 post calling for Thanksgiving to be canceled as a celebration of colonialism, Hong said she would not support doing so. "I'm not going to cancel Thanksgiving, but I know I'm going to be fighting the Republicans who are voting on policies that are making Thanksgiving dinners more expensive," she said. On a 2021 post saying police exist to uphold white supremacy, Hong said she does not support defunding police. "The governor cannot defund the police, and I won't defund the police," she said, adding that she supports investments in crime prevention and law enforcement training. Tiffany has called her "a card-carrying socialist committed to abolishing the police, the Senate, and prisons," and has criticized her appearances with Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar and online streamer Hasan Piker. Hong said she does not embrace the full national platform of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). "I have concerns around abolishing the Senate," she said. "We have an opportunity to elect candidates like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed into the Senate to fight for issues like Medicare for All. I don't want us to miss out on opportunities to deliver for working class people. So that is where I disagree with the platform." Yet, her answers have drawn criticism from some Democrats. Former Obama adviser David Axelrod wrote on X that "many people watching are going to conclude that if she is our nominee, we're going to lose Wisconsin," after Hong declined to directly disavow her Thanksgiving post during a CNN interview. Axelrod had earlier described the primary as "a slow-rolling car headed for a cliff." Crowley, Hong's chief rival, has also argued Democrats risk nominating a candidate who lacks the experience, record and coalition needed to win a statewide general election. She dismissed the criticism, arguing that her platform is broadly popular. "The issues, these are things that are electable, and the person who wins the most votes is the most electable," she said. "Fully funding public schools is a unifying universal electable issue." A Broader Democratic Debate after Michigan Her defense comes as Democrats continue debating the lessons of El-Sayed's narrow Michigan Senate primary victory over Representative Haley Stevens. El-Sayed won despite roughly $65 million in outside spending and a late endorsement of Stevens by Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer. "I believe the many overcoming the money," Hong said. But Democratic strategists like Axelrod said the Michigan result also highlighted the challenges facing candidates on the party's left flank. Speaking on NPR's Morning Edition, Axelrod said midterm elections often become referendums on the sitting president and warned that Republicans could use DSA membership and progressive allies to shift attention away from Trump and the economy. He noted that El-Sayed performed strongly among young and highly educated voters but struggled with rural and Black voters. "We are held to different standards," Hong said. "That's only going to motivate me to make sure to fight harder for the people of Wisconsin." Despite skepticism from some Democrats, Hong has led five consecutive Marquette University Law School polls. The latest survey, conducted July 22-27 among 407 Democratic primary voters, showed Hong with 38 percent support, followed by former Lieutenant Governor Mandela Barnes at 16 percent and Crowley at 7 percent, while 34 percent remained undecided. A State Navigate survey of 1,085 likely primary voters conducted July 23-26 and sponsored by UpNorthNews and Main Street Action showed Hong with 44 percent, followed by Crowley at 15 percent and Barnes at 14 percent. Barnes, however, ended his campaign on July 30. An internal poll released this week by Crowley's campaign showed Hong leading by 18 points. Hong's support has been strongest among younger voters. In last month's Marquette poll, 43 percent of Democratic primary voters ages 18 to 29 backed her, compared with 9 percent of voters 60 and older. She also won support from 45 percent of voters favorable toward democratic socialism, compared with 8 percent among those unfavorable toward the movement. The Marquette survey also found Trump's approval rating in Wisconsin at 40 percent, with 58 percent disapproving, his lowest mark in the poll during either term. Among likely voters, 84 percent of Democrats said they were certain to vote in November, compared with 79 percent of Republicans and 69 percent of independents. The general election is November 3. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Hong downplayed the electability question and told Newsweek why a democratic socialist can win a state Trump carried twice.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Former US President Biden's cancer has spread
news.text:
Former US president Joe Biden's cancer has metastasized further, according to his son Hunter Biden, who shared the update in a recent interview with the BBC.

In May 2025, just four months after he left office as the oldest sitting president, the elder Biden revealed he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones.

He subsequently began treatment, including radiation and hormone therapy, which the 83-year-old described as going "really well" last month, during an announcement of his upcoming memoir.

In a wide-ranging interview published late Friday with BBC Newsnight, Hunter Biden said his father's disease has spread despite the treatment.

"The cancer has spread, is metastasized into his bones and further," Biden said.

"It's very painful, and it's very debilitating in many respects, but he's still out there. He's still doing his thing...he so believes in this country."

Hunter Biden appeared to get emotional at times during the interview while discussing his father's health.

"It's really, really hard, and it's really sad to watch," he added.

Despite persistent questions about his health as the oldest-ever US president, Biden, then aged 81, decided to run for a second term in 2024.

Following a disastrous debate performance against Donald Trump in June 2024 and a wave of pressure from Democrats, Biden withdrew from the presidential race.

Trump went on to beat Biden's replacement candidate -- then-vice president Kamala Harris.

news.title: Why are Taylor Swift songs being removed from White House posts?
news.text:
The White House and a representative for Swift did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The removals come despite Swift having previously endorsed Trump’s Democratic rival, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, during the 2024 presidential election. Swift has not recently made public comments about Trump.
Trump has repeatedly criticized the singer. After Swift endorsed Harris in 2024, Trump wrote on social media: “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” He later questioned her popularity after making the remark.
The Trump campaign used two Swift songs during the past week on its TikTok account. One video referenced several of Swift’s well-known songs while pairing altered lyrics and titles with messages promoting Trump and criticizing the Biden-Harris administration.
Another video posted by the campaign in June used Swift’s “I Knew It, I Knew You,” a song from the soundtrack of “Toy Story 5.” The video showed Trump interacting with children at the White House, attending a UFC event and appearing at a campaign rally.
The use of Swift’s music is part of a broader pattern involving the Trump administration, which has featured popular songs in social media posts despite objections from some artists.
Artists including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have previously called on the administration not to use their music.
The White House also used Swift’s music in an April video showing the Artemis II crew meeting Trump. The video featured her song “High Infidelity.”
Another White House TikTok post in November featured “The Fate of Ophelia” from Swift’s album “The Life of a Showgirl,” alongside images of Trump, U.S. flags and national monuments.
That video generated widespread reaction online. A White House spokesperson later said the administration had created the post knowing that news organizations would amplify it.
Trump’s communications team has frequently used popular music alongside images of the president and his administration’s policies, including immigration enforcement, military operations and the arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
The latest removal of Swift’s songs adds another twist to the increasingly unusual relationship between the pop star’s music and Trump’s social media operation.

news.title: A view to  a kill
news.text:
The Trump administration recently issued a 123-page report heralding a "new golden age" for U.S. science.

The key, said the report, published in the name of Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, was to ensure that the approval of federal research grants "rests purely on merit, not the political fashions of the day."

There isn't much to say about this goal, other than that the White House has some nerve. For years, dating back to the first Trump administration, I have been documenting all the steps Trump and his minions have taken to undermine American science.

Thanks to a group of University of California researchers who have gone to court to fight Trump's cancellation of their research grants, we now have the most explicit confessions by six federal agencies about how slipshod and partisan their actions have been.

They're the departments of Defense, Energy and Transportation, and the National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health and the National Endowment for the Humanities.

All were required by court order to stipulate how they came to their decisions. Those stipulations were filed in federal court in San Francisco on July 15. Taken together, the government admitted that it used non-scientific considerations, AI screens and illegal or unconstitutional consideration to terminate billions of dollars in grants.

It may be unusual for such forthright admissions of wrongdoing to come from an administration not known for scrupulous rectitude. In this case and others like it, however, the government's lawyers were under the gun of court orders to come clean.

"They admitted what was true," Erwin Chemerinsky, the dean of UC Berkeley's law school and lead counsel for the plaintiffs in the researchers' lawsuit, told me. In any event, he added, "It's not like the Trump administration was hiding what it was doing."

The White House assault on scientific grants is an integral part of its general blitzkrieg on U.S. science. In a one-year retrospective on the current Trump term published in January, Nature counted 5,844 grants canceled or suspended by the National Institutes of Health, and 1,996 by the National Science Foundation.

The cancellations were disproportionately aimed at projects concerned with "misinformation, vaccine hesitancy, infectious diseases and research on people from under-represented ethnic and gender groups."

Both the NIH and the NSF reduced the number of new grants it issued by about 25 percent, Nature found, strangling the pipeline of basic research that is crucial for seeding research and development by industry. The Environmental Protection Agency and NASA, both of which have been heavily involved in research on global warming, lost more than 20 percent of their staff during Trump's first year.

Deep cuts also were imposed on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, perhaps accounting for the inability of America's public health infrastructure to counteract the surge in measles cases and the eruption of cyclospora infections this year.

That brings us back to the stipulations the federal agencies filed in the UC researchers' lawsuit. The researchers scored an early victory in the case in June 2025, when federal Judge Rita F. Lin granted them a preliminary injunction reinstating the terminated grants. Lin has scheduled a hearing for Oct. 20 on whether to make her injunction permanent and grant the researchers summary judgment against the government.

The agencies' stipulations are part of the record Lin will consider then; they all include spreadsheets listing the terminated grants and the rationales for their terminations. In sum, they open a window into the administration's ideological preoccupations.

The longest list--nearly 370 spreadsheet pages--was filed by the NIH, a unit of the Department of Health and Human Services. The agency fingered grants for termination by searching for keywords and phrases in their applications such as "workforce diversity," "equity, diversity, inclusion," "sexual orientation," "scientific evidence," and "health equity."

Some grants, the NIH confessed, appeared on a list provided by DOGE, the purported budget-cutting department headed by Elon Musk. In general, the goal was to "terminate grants presumed to express viewpoints ... that HHS-NIH no longer wished to subsidize."

The National Science Foundation acknowledged that it relied in part on a three-page list of disfavored keywords and phrases provided by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), such as "advocacy," "climate action," "racism" and "gender preference." The National Endowment for the Humanities searched for terms such as "transgenderism," "green new deal social engineering policies" and "environmental justice."

The most notable and explicit confession, though perhaps the least surprising, came from the Department of Energy.

Referring to a list of grant terminations announced in October 2025, the agency admitted that it terminated or canceled 283 grants "solely" based on whether their recipients were in states that had cast its electoral college votes for Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and had two Democratic senators.

Meanwhile, 340 other grants from states that voted for Trump were left in place.

The agency said it didn't rely on "programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factors." In other words, grants from blue states were cut simply because they originated in blue states.

The confession is unsurprising because the Department of Energy had made almost identical confessions in two previous federal lawsuits. In a case brought last year by the city of St. Paul, Minn., Energy Secretary Christopher Wright acknowledged that seven grants were terminated based primarily on "whether the grantee was located in a 'Blue State.'" Similar grants for red states were unaffected, he said.

In January, federal Judge Amit P. Mehta of the District of Columbia ordered the grants reinstated.

The agency repeated the stipulation in a lawsuit brought this year by the American Institute of Chemical Engineers over 11 canceled grants. In June, Mehta ordered those grants reinstated.

Despite these confessions, department spokesman Ben Dietderich told me that "none of the termination decisions were based on political considerations." He said that Wright had "explained this numerous times in briefings on Capitol Hill."

In fact, Wright didn't explain things so much as conduct a master class in weaseling. In an April 17 exchange with Rep. Mike Levin (D-San Juan Capistrano), for example, he said that the blue state versus red state discrepancy was "a timing question, not a decision question. ... The selection of the decisions to be announced, not the decisions. ... The decisions were nonpolitical."

But of course the decisions, not the timing, were the subject of the stipulations.

What's perplexing is why major U.S. institutions have been reluctant to take the battle to the administration themselves.

As I reported last year, the UC faculty won a significant victory over Trump when Lin ordered the restoration of some $600 million in funding cuts and blocked a $1.2-billion fine the White House proposed to levy on UCLA for purported civil rights violations. (The White House abandoned its appeal of Lin's order in February.)

But UC as an institution played no direct part in that case or any of the others brought to challenge Trump's assault on the university.

"The University regularly evaluates its legal strategy, including in light of last week's disclosures, and takes action when it is in the best interests of UC, our community, and our state," the office of UC President James B. Milliken told me by email.

It's true that the university has signed on as a co-plaintiff in several lawsuits brought jointly by the Association of American Universities and two other associations representing big universities. In each case, however, it was nestled within a cloud of about a dozen other big institutions. The cases are really being run by the associations.

Among educational institutions, Chemerinsky points out, only Harvard has stood up for itself in court--and has been successful, thus far. Meanwhile Columbia, Penn, Brown and others have made settlement deals.

"It's very disappointing that universities have settled with the Trump administration rather than going to court, and I think they would have won," he told me.

The same goes for other institutions that should have been expected to carry the fight: Nine major law firms targeted by Trump capitulated with settlements, but four firms have fought Trump and prevailed.

When the history of the Trump era is written, the institutional cowardice will deserve a chapter, and the courage of those that fought a chapter of their own.
news.author: Michael Hiltzik Los Angeles Times

news.title: Taylor Swift songs removed from Trump campaign, White House social media posts
news.text:
Taylor Swift's songs have been removed from social media videos posted by President Trump's campaign and the White House after appearing in TikTok posts over the past week. Swift has not spoken recently about Trump, though she endorsed his 2024 Democratic rival, then-Vice President Kamala Harris. 

Trump has repeatedly criticized Swift, writing "I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!" after her endorsement and later posting, "Has anyone noticed that, since I said 'I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,' she's no longer 'HOT?'"

The Trump campaign used two Swift songs on its TikTok page over the past week. One featured the caption, "Red (Donald Trump's Version). Red (Taylor Swift Wrote A Whole Album About Republicans)," referencing several of Swift's songs. A White House TikTok video posted four days earlier also used a Swift song, "August," over footage of Trump and First Lady Melania Trump watching fireworks, captioned, "Mood because it's August and Donald Trump is your president," along with the message, "I'm sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song!"

By Saturday, the audio had been removed, replaced with a message reading, "This sound isn't available."

The Trump campaign responded by posting a mock-up of Swift's "Red" album cover featuring Trump in his MAGA cap, captioned, "Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican Party." That track was also later removed from the account, with a message stating the copyright owner had not made the sound available.

Dozens of artists, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, have called on the Trump administration not to use their songs. The communications team has previously posted videos featuring hit songs alongside images of Trump's immigration crackdown, US military operations against Iran, and the arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
